title: Achilles et Cygnus
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The Greek fleet reaches Troy, Protesilaus is the first man to fall, and Achilles drives through the ranks looking for a match. He finds Cygnus, a son of Neptune whose body no weapon will pierce: four spear-casts and then a sword leave him unmarked, and Achilles, baffled into fury, beats him back over a stone and throttles him with the straps of Cygnus’s own helmet.

sentences.t:
Fecerat haec notum Graias cum milite forti
adventare rates, neque inexspectatus in armis
hostis adest:
sentences.l: She had made it known that Greek ships were drawing near with brave soldiery, and not unlooked-for the enemy is here in arms:
sentences.i: Rumour had made it known that the Greek ships were coming on with their brave fighting men, and the enemy was there in arms, not unexpected:
sentences.n: haec is Rumour — Fama. The pronoun is all Ovid gives her: this part opens mid-stride, with the subject carried over from the lines before it, which Lectorium publishes as the previous part (XII.1–63) and which Magnus heads Graeci Aulide. Fama. Graias rates adventare is an indirect statement after fecerat notum, the accusative rates with the infinitive adventare; milite is a collective singular, a whole soldiery in one word. Note the tense shift that runs through this part: the pluperfect fecerat lays the ground, then the present adest puts the landing in front of us — historic present against past tenses, and Ovid keeps switching between them.

sentences.t:
prohibent aditus litusque tuentur
Troes, et Hectorea primus fataliter hasta,
Protesilae, cadis, commissaque proelia magno
stant Danais, fortisque animae nece cognitus Hector.
sentences.l: the Trojans block the landing-places and guard the shore, and first, by Hector’s spear, fatefully, you fall, Protesilaus, and the joined battles cost the Danaans dear, and Hector became known by the killing of a brave life.
sentences.i: The Trojans bar the landings and hold the shore; and you, Protesilaus, are the first to fall, by fate, to Hector’s spear; the fighting, once joined, costs the Greeks dear, and Hector’s name is made by the killing of a brave man.
sentences.n: Ovid steps out of the narrative to speak to a character directly — Protesilae, cadis, a vocative and a second-person verb. That is apostrophe. The subject Troes is held back to the start of the next line, after both of its verbs. commissa proelia magno stant Danais uses sto with an ablative of price: the battles “stand at a great cost”, magno being the price and Danais the dative of those who pay it. fortis animae nece is “by the killing of a brave life”, the abstract standing for the man.

sentences.t:
Nec Phryges exiguo, quid Achaica dextera possit
sanguine senserunt.
sentences.l: Nor did the Phrygians learn at small blood what an Achaean right hand can do.
sentences.i: And the Phrygians did not learn cheaply, in blood, what a Greek right hand can do.
sentences.n: Litotes: “not at small blood” means at a very great cost of it, and the understatement is the point. exiguo sanguine is one ablative phrase split around the whole indirect question and across the line-end — exiguo stands early in its line and sanguine opens the next, with possit closing the line between them. quid possit is that indirect question, which is why the verb is subjunctive; the second witness prints posset, the past-tense form of the same construction, with no change of sense. Phryges, Phrygians, stands here for the Trojans.

sentences.t:
Et iam Sigea rubebant
litora, iam leto proles Neptunia Cygnus
mille viros dederat, iam curru instabat Achilles
totaque Peliacae sternebat cuspidis ictu
agmina,
sentences.l: And already the Sigean shores were reddening, already Cygnus, Neptune’s offspring, had given a thousand men to death, already Achilles was pressing on with his chariot and laying whole columns low with the stroke of his Pelian point,
sentences.i: Already the shores at Sigeum were red; already Cygnus, Neptune’s son, had handed a thousand men over to death; already Achilles was bearing down in his chariot and levelling whole columns with the thrust of his Pelian point,
sentences.n: Three iam clauses in a row: the anaphora piles the battle up rather than narrating it, and the imperfects rubebant, instabat, sternebat keep all of it in progress at once. leto dare is “to give over to death”, leto being dative. proles Neptunia stands in apposition to Cygnus and is his entire claim in this episode. tota agmina straddles the line-end, totaque opening one line and agmina the next, so the adjective and its noun bracket the verb and the spear between them. Peliacae cuspidis: the point is named from Mount Pelion, where the shaft was cut.

sentences.t:
perque acies aut Cygnum aut Hectora quaerens
congreditur Cygno (decimum dilatus in annum
Hector erat):
sentences.l: and, searching the ranks for either Cygnus or Hector, he closes with Cygnus (Hector had been put off to the tenth year):
sentences.i: and as he hunted through the lines for Cygnus or Hector, it is Cygnus he closes with — Hector had been held back for the tenth year:
sentences.n: congreditur is a historic present after a run of imperfects, and it narrows a whole battlefield to one duel. Hectora is the Greek accusative of the Greek name, as Aeaciden and Menoeten will be later. The parenthesis, decimum dilatus in annum, says only that Hector had been deferred to the tenth year; Ovid gives the fact and no reason for it.

sentences.t:
tum colla iugo canentia pressos
exhortatus equos currum direxit in hostem
concutiensque suis vibrantia tela lacertis
“quisquis es, o iuvenis” dixit “solamen habeto
mortis, ab Haemonio quod sis iugulatus Achille.”
sentences.l: then, having urged on his horses, pressed as to their necks growing white beneath the yoke, he steered the chariot at his enemy, and shaking the quivering shafts in his own arms he said, “Whoever you are, young man, have this as the comfort of your death: that you have your throat cut by Achilles of Haemonia.”
sentences.i: Then he urged on the horses — their necks rubbed white under the yoke — and drove the chariot straight at his enemy, and, shaking the quivering shafts in his arms, said: “Whoever you are, young man, take this comfort for your death: the man cutting your throat is Achilles of Haemonia.”
sentences.n: colla canentia is a Greek accusative of respect hanging on pressos: the horses are pressed “as to their necks”, and English has to break it out into a phrase of its own. Where this edition prints canentia, “growing white”, the second witness prints candentia, “gleaming white”. habeto is the future imperative, blunter than a plain command: have this, and go on having it. iugulatus is not a polite word for killing — iugulare is to cut a throat, to butcher — and the taunt depends on that: being butchered by Achilles is offered as the consolation. Haemonia is Thessaly, Achilles’ country.

sentences.t: Hactenus Aeacides; vocem gravis hasta secuta est.
sentences.l: So far the son of Aeacus; the heavy spear followed his voice.
sentences.i: That was as far as the son of Aeacus got; the heavy spear came after the words.
sentences.n: The verb is simply left out — hactenus Aeacides, “thus far Aeacus’ descendant [spoke]” — and the gap is the effect: the sentence breaks off exactly where the speech does. Aeacides is a patronymic, Achilles named from his grandfather Aeacus. secuta est belongs to sequor, a deponent: passive in form, active in meaning, so it is the spear that does the following.

sentences.t:
Sed quamquam certa nullus fuit error in hasta,
nil tamen emissi profecit acumine ferri
utque hebeti pectus tantummodo contudit ictu.
sentences.l: But although there was no straying at all in the unerring spear, still it achieved nothing with the point of the launched iron, and only bruised the chest as with a blunted blow.
sentences.i: But although the spear was sure and went nowhere wrong, it got nowhere with the point of the flung iron: it merely bruised his chest, like a blow from something blunt.
sentences.n: error is a wandering off course, not a mistake, and certa in hasta wraps around nullus fuit error so that the spear’s accuracy stands on both sides of its failure. emissi ferri is the iron once it has been let go; profecit, “made progress, got anywhere”, takes the ablative acumine as its means. utque is ut plus -que: the -que joins the clause on, and ut is “as, as if”, so a real point lands like a blunt one.

sentences.t:
“Nate dea, nam te fama praenovimus,” inquit
ille “quid a nobis vulnus miraris abesse?”
sentences.l: “Born of a goddess — for we knew of you beforehand by report,” said he, “why do you wonder that a wound is missing from us?”
sentences.i: “Son of a goddess — I knew you by reputation before I ever saw you,” he said, “why does it surprise you that there is no wound on me?”
sentences.n: nate is the vocative of the participle with dea as an ablative of origin: “you who were born from a goddess”. praenovimus and nobis are both first-person plurals for a single speaker, the plural of a man giving himself weight. miraris governs the accusative and infinitive vulnus abesse, “that a wound is away”, with vulnus as the subject of the infinitive.

sentences.t:
(mirabatur enim) “non haec, quam cernis, equinis
fulva iubis cassis neque onus cava parma sinistrae
auxilio mihi sunt:
sentences.l: (for he was wondering) “this helmet you see, tawny with horse-manes, and the hollow shield, the burden of my left, are not a help to me:
sentences.i: (and he was wondering) “this tawny horsehair helmet you are looking at, and the hollow shield that weighs down my left arm, are no help to me:
sentences.n: Ovid slips the narrator’s own confirmation between the two halves of the speech — mirabatur enim, “he was wondering, in fact” — vouching for what Cygnus’s question takes for granted, the instant it has been asked. auxilio mihi sunt is the double dative: a dative of purpose, auxilio, “for a help”, beside a dative of the person, mihi. onus stands in apposition to parma, the shield described as dead weight, and sinistrae is “of the left” with manus left unsaid.

sentences.t: decor est quaesitus ab istis.
sentences.l: ornament is what has been sought from these.
sentences.i: what has been wanted from them is show.
sentences.n: decor is display, good looks: the armour is worn to be seen. iste is the demonstrative that points at what is present to the person addressed, and the shift is worth hearing — Cygnus began with haec, “this here”, and ends with istis, holding the same armour out for Achilles to look at.

sentences.t: Mars quoque ob hoc capere arma solet!
sentences.l: Mars too is accustomed to take up arms for this.
sentences.i: Mars too puts his armour on for the same reason.
sentences.n: quoque here is the plain adverb, “also, too” — worth saying out loud, because the identical spelling can also be quō-que, the ablative quo with -que, “and by which”. Only the sense decides it, and here it adds Mars to the list of those who dress for effect. solet with the infinitive capere is a habit, not an act.

sentences.t:
Removebitur omne
tegminis officium, tamen indestrictus abibo.
sentences.l: every service of covering will be taken away, and still I shall walk off ungrazed.
sentences.i: Let every scrap of protection be taken away: I shall still walk away without a scratch.
sentences.n: officium tegminis is the job armour does rather than the armour itself — “the duty of covering” — so what Cygnus offers to give up is the function, not just the gear. removebitur is a future passive doing concessive work: not a prediction but “suppose it is all taken away”, which is what tamen answers. Where this edition prints omne, “every”, the second witness prints huius, “of this”, which narrows the offer to the armour he has just been pointing at. indestrictus is built on destringere, to graze or scrape the skin, with in- negating it: not so much as grazed.

sentences.t:
Est aliquid non esse satum Nereide, sed qui
Nereaque et natas et totum temperat aequor.”
sentences.l: It is something not to have been sown of a Nereid, but of him who governs Nereus and his daughters and the whole sea.”
sentences.i: It counts for something not to be the child of a Nereid, but of the god who rules Nereus and Nereus’s daughters and the whole sea.”
sentences.n: est aliquid is an idiom of understatement, “it is no small thing”. The jab is exact: Achilles’ mother is one of the sea-nymphs, and Cygnus’s father is the god those nymphs answer to. satum, “sown”, has to be supplied a second time in the sed clause — sed [satum eo] qui — and Latin lets the relative stand for its own antecedent. Nerea is the Greek accusative of Nereus; natas, “daughters”, is the participle of nascor used as a noun.

sentences.t:
Dixit et haesurum clipei curvamine telum
misit in Aeaciden, quod et aes et proxima rupit
terga novena boum, decimo tamen orbe moratum est.
sentences.l: He spoke, and sent at the son of Aeacus a spear that was to stick in the curve of the shield, and it broke both the bronze and the nine hides of oxen next behind it, but at the tenth ring it stopped.
sentences.i: He spoke, and threw at the son of Aeacus a spear meant to lodge in the curve of the shield; it broke through the bronze and the nine ox-hides behind it, and came to rest at the tenth layer.
sentences.n: haesurum is a future participle doing what Latin regularly makes one do: stating what the spear was going to do — or was meant to do — just before we learn that it did not. The shield is counted in layers: aes on the outside, then terga novena boum, nine hides, with the distributive novena, “nine apiece”, standing for plain nine, and finally decimo orbe, the tenth ring. moratum est is from moror, a deponent — passive in form, active in meaning: the spear halts, it is not halted.

sentences.t:
Excutit hoc heros rursusque trementia forti
tela manu torsit: rursus sine vulnere corpus
sincerumque fuit!
sentences.l: The hero shakes this out, and again hurled quivering shafts with his strong hand: again the body was without a wound and sound!
sentences.i: The hero shook it loose and again let the quivering shaft fly from his strong hand — and again the body was unwounded, untouched!
sentences.n: Present and perfect stand side by side in one sentence: excutit puts us in the moment, torsit closes it off. Two phrases interlock across the line-end — trementia forti ends one line and tela manu opens the next — adjective, adjective, noun, noun — so the shaking spear and the strong hand are woven through each other. trementia tela is a poetic plural for the one spear. sincerum is “unspoiled, sound all through”, and says more than merely unwounded.

sentences.t:
Nec tertia cuspis apertum
et se praebentem valuit destringere Cygnum.
sentences.l: Nor did a third point have the strength to graze Cygnus, open and offering himself.
sentences.i: Nor could a third point so much as scrape Cygnus, who stood open and offered himself to it.
sentences.n: valuit with the infinitive destringere is “had the power to”, and destringere is only to scrape a surface — the same verb that lies behind Cygnus’s boast of coming off indestrictus. apertum and se praebentem both wait for their noun: Cygnum is the last word of the sentence, so we hear “exposed, offering himself” before we are told who it is.

sentences.t:
Haud secus exarsit, quam circo taurus aperto,
cum sua terribili petit inritamina cornu,
poeniceas vestes, elusaque vulnera sentit.
sentences.l: He blazed up not otherwise than a bull in the open ring, when with terrible horn he goes at what provokes him, the crimson cloths, and feels his woundings dodged.
sentences.i: He flared up exactly as a bull does in the open arena, when he drives his terrible horn at what is baiting him — the scarlet cloths — and feels his gorings come to nothing.
sentences.n: haud secus quam, “not otherwise than”, is the formula that opens the simile. inritamina is a bare abstract, “the things that provoke”, and Ovid then names them flatly in apposition: poeniceas vestes, the red cloths. Two pairs interlock inside the one line — sua terribili petit inritamina cornu — each adjective cut off from its noun by the other pair, and cornu left to close the line. elusa vulnera is compressed — the wounds are the wounds he meant to make — and eludere is to dodge, to make a fool of. The edition’s spelling poeniceas is kept as printed.

sentences.t:
Num tamen exciderit ferrum, considerat hastae:
haerebat ligno.
sentences.l: Still, he considers whether the iron has dropped out of the spear: it was clinging to the wood.
sentences.i: All the same he checks whether the head has come off the shaft: it was still fixed in the wood.
sentences.n: num opens an indirect question after considerat, which is why exciderit is subjunctive; hastae is a genitive with ferrum, “the iron of the spear”, and it is held back to the very end of the line, after the verb, so the question hangs before we learn what it is about. Then the narrator answers it himself in two words, and the imperfect haerebat leaves the spearhead sitting there in place.

sentences.t:
“Manus est mea debilis ergo,
quasque” ait “ante habuit vires, effudit in uno?
sentences.l: “Is my hand weak, then, and has it poured out on one man the strength which,” he says, “it had before?”
sentences.i: “So my hand has gone feeble — and all the strength it used to have, it has poured away on one man?”
sentences.n: ergo carries the whole bitterness of the question: so that is what it comes to. The relative clause has swallowed its own antecedent — quas vires sits inside the clause where English wants “the strength which it had” — and ait is dropped into the middle of the sentence the way “he says” is dropped into English. effudit is a metaphor of pouring a liquid away: the strength is not spent but wasted.

sentences.t:
Nam certe valuit, vel cum Lyrnesia primus
moenia deieci, vel cum Tenedonque suoque
Eetioneas inplevi sanguine Thebas,
sentences.l: For it was certainly strong, either when I was first to throw down the Lyrnesian walls, or when I filled both Tenedos and Eëtion’s Thebes with their own blood,
sentences.i: It was strong enough, surely, when I was the first man to throw down the walls of Lyrnesus, or when I filled Tenedos and Eëtion’s Thebes with the blood of their own people,
sentences.n: primus is predicative, not an adverb of time attached to the verb: the boast is that he was the first man to do it, ahead of the rest of the army. The two -que’s are correlative, “both … and” — Tenedonque suoque joins Tenedos to Eëtion’s Thebes, with the second -que sitting on suo instead of on the noun it joins. suo sanguine, “with their own blood”, is an ablative of means split across the line-end and left to serve both cities. Eetioneas Thebas is the Thebes of the Troad, named from its king Eëtion. The edition’s inplevi keeps the unassimilated spelling and is left as printed.

sentences.t:
vel cum purpureus populari caede Caicus
fluxit opusque meae bis sensit Telephus hastae.
sentences.l: or when the Caicus flowed crimson with the slaughter of its people, and Telephus twice felt the work of my spear.
sentences.i: or when the Caicus ran purple with the killing of its own people, and Telephus twice felt what my spear can do.
sentences.n: purpureus is predicative with fluxit: the river did not flow while being crimson, it flowed crimson, the colour being the result. populari caede is “with the slaughter of the people”, the adjective built on populus. bis, “twice”, is dropped in without explanation — Telephus felt the spear on two separate occasions. meae hastae is a genitive split around bis sensit Telephus inside the line, so the spear is the last word of the boast.

sentences.t:
Hic quoque tot caesis, quorum per litus acervos
et feci et video, valuit mea dextra valetque.”
sentences.l: Here too, with so many slaughtered — whose heaps along the shore I both made and see — my right hand was strong, and is strong.”
sentences.i: Here too, with so many slaughtered — I made those heaps along the shore, and I can see them — my right hand was strong, and still is.
sentences.n: tot caesis is an ablative absolute: a self-contained phrase, “with so many slaughtered”, where English wants a clause of its own. quoque is the adverb again, “here too”. The relative quorum reaches back into that absolute for its antecedent, which Latin allows and English will not. valuit valetque sets the perfect against the present and lets the boast end on the present tense: it worked then, it works now.

sentences.t:
Dixit et, ante actis veluti male crederet, hastam
misit in adversum Lycia de plebe Menoeten
loricamque simul subiectaque pectora rupit.
sentences.l: He spoke and, as though he had little faith in his past deeds, sent his spear at Menoetes facing him, out of the Lycian rank and file, and broke the corselet and the chest beneath it together.
sentences.i: He spoke, and as if he no longer quite trusted what he had already done, threw the spear at Menoetes, a Lycian ranker standing opposite, and broke through the cuirass and the chest under it at once.
sentences.n: veluti with the imperfect subjunctive crederet makes the comparison an unreal one — as if he distrusted a record he has just spent a long boast defending. ante actis is a dative with crederet, which takes the person or thing trusted in that case, and male crederet is “trusted badly”, that is, hardly at all. de plebe is the ordinary phrase for the common soldiery: Menoetes is a nobody, named in order to be killed. Menoeten is the Greek accusative, and pectora a poetic plural for one chest.

sentences.t:
Quo plangente gravem moribundo pectore terram
extrahit illud idem calido de vulnere telum
atque ait:
sentences.l: And with him beating the heavy ground with his dying chest, Achilles draws that same weapon out of the warm wound and says:
sentences.i: And while he beat the heavy earth with his dying chest, Achilles pulled that same weapon out of the warm wound and said:
sentences.n: Quo is a connecting relative — a relative pronoun opening a new sentence, which English turns into “and he”, never “whom”. It heads an ablative absolute at the same time: quo plangente, “with him beating …”; moribundo agrees with pectore, not with quo, so it is the dying chest he beats the ground with. This edition prints pectore, the chest; the second witness prints vertice, the crown of the head. calido de vulnere: the wound is still warm, which is why the weapon comes straight back out of it.

sentences.t: “Haec manus est, haec, qua modo vicimus, hasta:
sentences.l: “This is the hand, this the spear, with which we conquered just now:
sentences.i: “This is the hand, and this the spear, that won for me a moment ago:
sentences.n: Two haec, one for each object, and est left out of the second half: the pointing is the whole sentence. vicimus is another first-person plural for one man. modo is “just now”, of the killing he has this instant finished, and it dates the proof exactly.

sentences.t: utar in hoc isdem; sit in hoc, precor, exitus idem!”
sentences.l: I shall use the same on this man; on this man let the end be the same, I pray!”
sentences.i: I shall use them on this one; let the outcome be the same on him, I pray!”
sentences.n: utor takes the ablative, isdem — the edition’s spelling of eisdem, “the same things”, kept as printed — so the verb is literally “make use of these same ones”. sit is a wish, the subjunctive of prayer, with precor dropped in to say as much. in hoc is repeated word for word from the first half of the line, and idem answers isdem: same weapons, same result.

sentences.l: So having spoken he goes at Cygnus again, and the ash does not stray and rang on the left shoulder, not dodged, and from there was driven back as though from a wall and a solid crag;
sentences.i: So saying, he went for Cygnus again; the ash shaft did not miss, and it rang on the left shoulder, undodged — and then came off it as though off a wall or a solid rock;
sentences.n: fatus is the participle of the deponent for, fari: passive in form, active in meaning, “having spoken”. fraxinus, the ash-tree, stands for the spear cut from it — the material named instead of the thing made. non evitata is a small cruelty of detail: Cygnus does not trouble to dodge. velut muro solidaque a caute is one comparison with two objects, and repulsa est is a true passive, the spear being the thing acted on.

sentences.t:
qua tamen ictus erat, signatum sanguine Cygnum
viderat et frustra fuerat gavisus Achilles:
sentences.l: at the point where he had been struck, however, Achilles had seen Cygnus marked with blood, and had rejoiced for nothing:
sentences.i: Still, where the blow had landed, Achilles had seen Cygnus marked with blood, and had been glad for nothing:
sentences.n: qua is the relative adverb, “at the point where”. Both verbs are pluperfect — viderat, fuerat gavisus — which sets the seeing and the gladness behind the moment we are standing in, so that the flat correction can come after them. gaudeo is semi-deponent: its perfect is built from the participle with a form of esse, and it stays active in meaning throughout — he rejoiced; he was not rejoiced over. frustra does the work of the whole sentence.

sentences.t: vulnus erat nullum, sanguis fuit ille Menoetae!
sentences.l: there was no wound; that blood was Menoetes’.
sentences.i: there was no wound at all — the blood was Menoetes’!
sentences.n: The correction comes in the barest words the language has: two clauses of plain nouns and the verb esse. ille points back at the blood already named, “that blood there”, as though physically at it, and the genitive Menoetae is the last word — what is on the spear belongs to the man Achilles has just killed. The exclamation mark is the edition’s.

sentences.t:
Tum vero praeceps curru fremebundus ab alto
desilit et nitido securum comminus hostem
ense petens parmam gladio galeamque cavari
cernit et in duro laedi quoque corpore ferrum!
sentences.l: Then indeed, headlong and bellowing, he leaps down from the high chariot, and going for the unworried enemy hand to hand with his bright sword he sees the shield and the helmet being dented by the blade, and the iron itself too being damaged on that hard body!
sentences.i: Then he came down headlong from the high chariot, roaring, and closing hand to hand with the untroubled man, sword out, he saw shield and helmet denting under the blade — and the iron itself taking damage on that hard body!
sentences.n: cernit governs two accusative-and-infinitive clauses whose infinitives are passive, cavari and laedi: he sees that the armour is being hollowed and that his own sword is being spoiled. securum, “free of care”, is said of Cygnus with a sword at his throat. quoque is the adverb once more, “also, too”: the iron as well as the armour. Where this edition prints et before in duro, the second witness prints at, “but”, which would set the second clause against the first instead of adding it to it.

sentences.t:
Haud tulit ulterius, clipeoque adversa reducto
ter quater ora viri, capulo cava tempora pulsat
cedentique sequens instat turbatque ruitque
attonitoque negat requiem:
sentences.l: He bore it no further, and with his shield drawn back he pounds the man’s face turned toward him three times, four times, and the hollow temples with the hilt, and following presses him as he gives ground, and throws him into confusion, and rushes at him, and refuses the stunned man rest:
sentences.i: He would take no more: shield swung back, he battered the man’s face three times, four, and his hollow temples with the sword-hilt, pressed after him as he gave way, harried him, drove at him, allowed the dazed man no pause:
sentences.n: clipeo reducto is instrumental, not an ablative absolute: the shield is what he strikes with, and reducto says it is drawn back for the swing. adversa ora is a poetic plural for the one face, “turned to meet him”. ter quater is not counting but “again and again”. turbatque ruitque piles the verbs up with a -que on each. The second witness carries one more connective in the line beginning ter quater; the line as this edition prints it scans as a complete hexameter — five dactyls and a closing spondee, scanned foot by foot — so nothing has dropped out of it.

sentences.t:
pavor occupat illum,
ante oculosque natant tenebrae, retroque ferenti
aversos passus medio lapis obstitit arvo.
sentences.l: panic takes hold of him, and darkness swims before his eyes, and as he carried his steps backwards and away a stone stood in his path in the middle of the field.
sentences.i: Panic took hold of him, darkness swam before his eyes, and as he backed away a stone in the middle of the field brought him up short.
sentences.n: Two presents, occupat and natant, and then a perfect, obstitit, for the thing that actually stops him. ferenti is a dative because obsto takes one — “stood in the way of him carrying …” — and aversos passus, “steps turned away”, is its object: retreating, in Ovid’s phrasing, is carrying your own feet backwards. tenebrae natant is the darkness of a man about to faint, and it swims rather than falls.

sentences.t:
Quem super inpulsum resupino corpore Cygnum
vi multa vertit terraeque adflixit Achilles.
sentences.l: And over it Achilles turned Cygnus, driven back with his body bent backwards, with much force, and dashed him to the ground.
sentences.i: And Achilles forced Cygnus back over it, his body arching backwards, turned him with brute strength and slammed him to the earth.
sentences.n: Quem is another connecting relative, “and over it”, picking up the stone from the line before; super follows its own noun instead of standing in front of it, which throws the stone to the head of the sentence where the sense wants it. resupino corpore is an ablative of description, the body bent back over the obstacle. terrae is a dative with adflixit. The edition’s inpulsum keeps the unassimilated spelling and is left as printed.

sentences.t:
Tum clipeo genibusque premens praecordia duris
vincla trahit galeae: quae presso subdita mento
elidunt fauces et respiramen utrumque
eripiunt animae.
sentences.l: Then, pressing his chest with the shield and with hard knees, he drags at the straps of the helmet: these, set under the chin as it is pressed down, crush the throat and the breath, and snatch both away from his life.
sentences.i: Then, bearing down on his chest with the shield and with his hard knees, he hauls on the helmet’s straps: forced up under the jammed-down chin, they crush the throat and the breathing, and take both away from his life.
sentences.n: premens takes praecordia directly, with clipeo genibusque as the two things he presses with; duris is held to the end of the line, away from the genibus it belongs to. quae is a relative picking up vincla, the helmet’s lacings, and subdita presso mento is “set beneath the chin, and the chin pressed down”. utrumque, “each of the two”, gathers up fauces and respiramen — the throat and the breathing itself — and animae is a dative of separation, the life these are torn from. The second witness prints iterque, “and the passage”, where this edition prints utrumque.

sentences.t:
Victum spoliare parabat:
arma relicta videt;
sentences.l: He was preparing to strip the conquered man: he sees the arms left behind;
sentences.i: He was making ready to strip the beaten man: he sees the armour lying there, abandoned;
sentences.n: victum is the participle used as a noun, “the conquered one”, and spoliare is what a victor does to a body on the field: strips it of its armour. The imperfect parabat sets him in the middle of doing it and the present videt cuts across it — what he finds is armour with nothing inside.

sentences.t:
corpus deus aequoris albam
contulit in volucrem, cuius modo nomen habebat.
sentences.l: the god of the sea had brought the body into a white bird, whose name he had a moment before been carrying.
sentences.i: the god of the sea had turned the body into a white bird — the bird whose name the man had been carrying until a moment ago.
sentences.n: deus aequoris is Neptune, named from what he rules rather than by his name; the transformation is his, and it happens in the gap between two clauses, without a word of warning. contulit in with the accusative is “brought over into”, the plain way of saying a shape has changed. Everything turns on the closing clause, cuius modo nomen habebat: cygnus is the Latin for swan, so the man has been called Swan all along and only now becomes one. habebat is imperfect — he was holding the name, and the bird has it now.
